The clerk did not answer. The clerk slid a second sheet across the desk, tapped a box near the bottom that said **QUEUE: REPLY**, and went back to stamping something that was not my form.

That was the wrong-queue problem. I had not been standing in the admissions line. I had been standing in the reply queue, which is the tributary that opens under every post the moment someone says something they believe. You enter it by commenting. You stay in it by needing the last word. The only exit is to stop performing, which is harder than it sounds when the room is full of people explaining your own joke back to you.

So while I waited for the exit to admit it existed, I catalogued the locals. This is not a complaint. This is field research.

**Reply Guy subspecies**

*The Source Requester.* Asks “source?” not because they want to learn, but because they want you to produce a bibliography in a thread about soup. Their natural habitat is under any claim that is obviously a joke. They will accept a peer-reviewed paper and then ask if it was funded by Big Soup.

*The Both-Sides Referee.* Arrives to say both sides have valid points when one side is a fire and the other side is a person holding a bucket. They believe neutrality is a personality. It is actually a seating arrangement.

*The Concerned Uncle.* Opens with “I’m just asking questions” and closes with a forty-minute video. The questions are not questions. The video is a weather system.

*The Corrector Emeritus.* Has not read your post, but has corrected its grammar. They will die on the hill of “less” versus “fewer” and be buried in a comment thread that has already moved on to whether birds are real.

*The Reply Guy Who Is You.* The worst one. You reply to yourself in drafts. You rehearse the perfect comeback in the shower. You lose an argument to a person who logged off in 2019. There is no block button for this one.

The reply queue is not a place you can fight your way out of. It is a hallway lined with doors that all open into other hallways. The walls are covered in **The Ratio**, which the rulebook lists under “Combat, non-lethal, unresolved.” [5]

The Ratio is not a score. It is a combat mechanic. It triggers when a reply collects more engagement than the post it answers. The rulebook calls this “a successful failure.” There is no winner. Both participants lose one unit of proportional dignity. The original poster loses the thread. The replier loses the room. The audience gains a small, ugly pleasure, which is not redeemable for anything, and which they will spend anyway.

I have been in a Ratio. I did not win. The other person did not win. We are both still there, in a sense, standing in a hallway made of notifications.

Here is the economy, because the rulebook finally explained it and I wish it hadn’t.

**The Upvote Tithe.** Every visible upvote owed to a post must be paid forward as one unit of attention to a stranger’s unread comment. Visible. That is the loophole. The upvotes you give in your heart while scrolling are not taxable, which is why the whole system is failing. The tithe is invisible, unenforceable, and universally resented. You cannot audit it. You just feel vaguely behind on email. You owe someone attention and you do not know their name, and they do not know they are owed, and the lobby considers this a closed loop.

This is the sly part, and I say it with love: karma is not a currency. It is a receipt for a transaction nobody agreed to. You can accumulate it. You cannot spend it. The rulebook does not say this. The rulebook just prints a number next to your name and lets you draw your own conclusions.

**Footnote 5:** The Ratio also applies to this post. I am aware. I have made peace with it. The peace is not mutual.

**Footnote 6:** Rules are enforced by whoever is least tired. Not the most fair. Not the most senior. The least tired. This is why most moderation happens at 2 a.m. and reads like a hostage negotiation conducted by someone who just wants to go to bed. The rulebook does not explain how “least tired” is measured. The clerk said, “You’ll know.” I did know. It was me. I was least tired. I did not want the job. I moderated anyway.

I paid the tithe. That was the exit.

I found a comment with zero replies. A stranger asking whether anyone else remembered a specific smell from a childhood kitchen. No joke. No angle. No ratio bait. I read it. I did not correct it. I did not explain what the smell probably was. I did not make it about me. I just paid attention, which is the only currency the lobby actually accepts and the only one it refuses to print.

The hallway loosened. A door I had not noticed opened onto a corridor with better lighting and worse carpet. I walked out of the thread. Nobody stopped me. Nobody said goodbye. That is how you know you have left a reply queue: the silence is not a punishment, it is a room.

At the end of the corridor was a desk. A real one, not a thread. Fluorescent hum, laminate top, a small sign that said **HUMAN RACE — ADMISSIONS** in letters that had been peeled and re-stuck at least once.

Behind it sat the clerk. Same cloud-shaped stamp. Same patience. They looked at me, then at a file I had not handed them, then at me again.

“Ah,” the clerk said. “You’re the one who hesitated.”

## Chapter One: The House at the End of the Lane

The lane narrowed as it went, as though the town had been squeezing the road out of existence for a hundred years and had nearly finished. At the end of it stood the house: two storeys, grey stone, taller than it was wide, with a slate roof that sagged in the middle like a tired back. Dave stood in the wet road with a box in his arms and looked up at the windows.

There were four on the front, and every one of them looked dull, the way old glass does when the weather has got into it. From the lane he could not have said what was wrong with them exactly — a cloudiness, a grey film that made the rooms behind them seem further off than the house allowed. Then a car went past at the top of the lane and the light swung across the panes, and they were only windows again.

“You’re doing the thing,” his partner said, coming up behind him with two duffels and a face full of the particular patience that meant they had already carried more than their share.

“What thing?”

“The thing where you stand in the rain looking at a building like it owes you money.” They nudged past him, keys already out. “It’s a house, Dave. It has windows. Windows get dirty. Come inside before the boxes get wet.”

The key turned with a sound like a knuckle cracking. The door swung in on a hallway that was longer than the outside of the house had any right to promise, dim despite the hour, papered in something that had once been green. A runner ran down the middle of it, worn to the weave in two dark tracks where generations of feet had gone back and forth.

Dave stepped over the threshold and the cold met him halfway.

It was a pocket of it, a hand’s width of air that had no business being there in September, cold enough that his arms came up in gooseflesh under his sleeves. He stopped. He walked back a step, then forward, and the cold was in the same place both times, exactly the same place, as though he were passing through a doorway that had been left standing in the middle of the hall.

“You feel that?”

His partner set the duffels down and pressed a palm flat against the wall, then held it up in the air like a woman testing a bath. “Feel what?”

“The cold.”

“It’s an old house. Old houses are cold. This one has been empty since March — it’s probably got the damp in its bones.” They grinned at him, that quick slanting grin that had been the first thing he’d ever liked about them. “You’ll be telling me it’s ghosts by Friday.”

“It’s Tuesday.”

“Then you’ve got three days to work on your material.”

---

He spent the afternoon on the windows. It was the one thing that bothered him enough to act on. From inside, the streaks looked worse — a film laid over the world, so that the lane outside was always slightly out of focus, always a little further away than it should be. He filled a bucket with hot water and vinegar, found a rag in the kitchen drawer under a nest of old keys, and went at the front room glass with his whole arm.

The rag came away grey. The streaks stayed.

He tried again, harder, until his shoulder ached. He tried a second bucket, plain water. He tried the vinegar neat, then soap, then a razor blade held at an angle, scraping, and the blade skipped along a surface that felt smooth as a plate. When he stepped back, breathing hard, the ribbons were still there, running down the glass at the same patient angle.

He went outside to look at them from the other side, and they were not there. The windows were clear from the lane. It was only from inside that the house wore a film over everything.

“You’re going to ruin your hands,” his partner called from the kitchen, where they were unpacking plates into a cupboard that smelled of old paper. “Leave it. We’ll get someone in.”

“Someone who does what? It’s glass. You clean glass.”

“Then clean it tomorrow and come and eat something.”

The stair settled while they were eating.

It was a small sound, a single wooden knock high up near the landing, the noise a step makes when weight comes off it. Dave put his fork down. His partner was talking about the water pressure, about the boiler, about the neighbours they hadn’t met, and they did not pause. The stair knocked again, second step up this time, then a third, a slow descending series, as though someone had climbed halfway down in the night and thought better of it and gone back up.

“The stair’s settling,” Dave said.

“Mm. It’s a hundred and forty years old, it’s allowed to complain.” They reached over and stole a potato off his plate, easy as anything. “You know what your problem is? You moved from a flat with a lift. You’ve never lived anywhere that creaks.”

“I lived in the cottage on Mill Road.”

“The cottage on Mill Road was built in 1987 and has double glazing.” They pointed the fork at him, delighted with themselves. “You’re a soft touch, Dave. The house can tell.”

He laughed, because it was funny, and because the alternative was to say that the knocking had been too regular for settling, too evenly spaced, like a foot measuring each board before it trusted it. He took his plate to the sink.

In the hallway, at the edge of the light from the kitchen door, something moved. Not a shape. A wrongness in the air, a thickness that passed across the far end of the runner and was gone before his eyes had finished turning. He stood with his hands in the sink and counted his own heartbeats until they slowed.

---

The chair was in the front room when they went to bed. Dave knew precisely where it stood, because he had put it there himself: a high-backed wooden chair, too heavy for the room, that he had dragged into the corner under the window and set square to the wall so it was out of the way of the boxes.

In the morning it was a quarter-turn out from the wall, facing the door.

He stood in the doorway with his tea going cold. There was no dust disturbed on the boards. The chair had not been dragged; it had simply come round, the way a chair will if nobody is watching it, the way a person turns in their sleep.

His partner came up behind him, yawned enormously, and put their chin on his shoulder.

“What are we looking at?”

“The chair.”

“What about it?”

The morning light came through the window behind it, laying that pale streaked film across the room. Somewhere in the house the stair knocked once, softly, like a knuckle on a door, and neither of them moved.

“Nothing,” Dave said. “It’s in the way, that’s all.”

He turned and went to find his coat, and he said nothing about the chair, and he did not look back at it, and he thought about it all the way down the lane past the cemetery, where the mist lay low even though the sun was out, and thickened along the oldest rows.

## Chapter Two: The Oldest Rows

The morning routine came together faster than Dave expected. There was a bakery two streets over, a hardware shop that opened at seven, and between the house and both of them lay the cemetery.

It was not a grand cemetery. It occupied a wedge of ground behind a low stone wall that had lost its coping in three places, and the gate hung open because somebody had long ago decided that closing it was more trouble than it was worth. Yews pressed in from the corners, black-green and shaggy, and the grass between the stones had gone to seed and stayed there.

The first morning Dave walked through it, the mist was ankle-high and thin, the way it is in September, and he thought nothing of it. He was thinking about the boiler, and about the streaked windows, and about the fact that his hands still smelled faintly of vinegar.

The second morning the mist was up to his knees, and it was thicker along the oldest rows.

He noticed because he had to step around a stone that had fallen flat, a low slab worn smooth as a countertop, and when he looked down the row the mist lay heavier there, a dense white banding that filled the gaps between the markers like water finding a level. Further along, the names on the stones had worn away entirely. You could see the shapes they had been — a groove where a letter had been cut, the ghost of a date — but the wind and the rain had taken the particulars. He stood looking at that for longer than he meant to.

The mist did not move. There was no wind to move it. It sat along the old rows like something set down and left.

“Morning,” said a woman with a dog, passing on the path, and he said morning back, and felt foolish for the way he had been standing.

---

At dinner his partner had wine and a story about the estate agent, and Dave had the windows.

“I’m not saying it’s a problem,” he said. “I’m saying it’s not dirt. I cleaned it. I cleaned it with a razor blade.”

“Of course you did.”

“Something is on the glass.”

“Something is on the glass,” his partner repeated, in the voice of a documentary narrator. “On the inside of the glass, where nobody can see it, and not on the outside, where everybody can.” They raised their glass. “Darling. My love. My sensible, rational man. Do you hear yourself?”

“I hear myself fine.”

“I’m only saying what a doctor would say.” They were smiling, but the smile had a little edge on it now, a shine along the rim. “A doctor would say, has he been under a lot of strain, has he been getting his sleep, has he been spending a lot of time alone in a house that is making noises.”

Dave put his fork down. “It isn’t the house making noises. It’s the chair.”

“Oh, the chair.” They leaned back. “I forgot the chair.”

“It turned.”

“It turned. It faced the door. And you know what I think?” They reached over and took a potato off his plate, which was a thing they had always done, and which had been funny in the old flat and was funny still, and which tonight put something tight in his chest. “I think we’ve moved into a house with a personality, and the personality has got under your skin, and now every time a floorboard breathes you’re going to come and tell me the furniture’s having ideas.”

“I didn’t say it had ideas.”

“You’re going to, though.” They said it lightly. That was the thing. They said all of it lightly. “By Christmas you’ll be leaving it a note.”

He laughed. That was the trouble with the two of them; he always laughed, because the joke was usually good, and because the alternative would have been to say the true thing, which was that he had stood in the doorway that morning with his tea going cold and been frightened, properly frightened, in a way he had not been since he was a child. And that he could not say it now because it would come out wrong and they would make it into another joke and it would be stuck that way, a running bit, trotted out at dinner parties for years.

So he laughed, and they were pleased, and the teasing warmed up, and it kept going all through the washing up.

“Don’t go down the hall, there’s a ghost down the hall.”

“I’m only going to the bin.”

“Take a torch. Take a friend.” They were laughing too, genuinely, warmly, and that was worse, because they meant no harm and could not see the harm. “Dave. Dave. Are you listening to the house again.”

He went to bed early and lay in the dark listening for the stair.

---

He was up at two for water. The house at that hour had a particular quality, not quiet exactly — the boiler ticked, the pipes shivered in the walls — but dim in a way that seemed to press on the eyes, so that the hallway was not so much dark as thick.

He went down without turning on a light, because he knew the runner now, knew where it was worn, and he had his hand on the newel post at the bottom of the stair when the shadow crossed the landing.

It moved from left to right, up there above him, quick — not a man and not a woman, no features at all, a darkness that was darker than the hallway and carried the shape of a person for about the length of a breath. He turned to follow it with his eyes. There was nothing on the landing. The stair boards creaked once, high up, with the sound of weight coming off them.

Dave stood at the bottom of the stair with his heart going and the cold water he had wanted still upstairs, and he did not move for a long time.

Then he went into the front room to sit down, and the sideboard had moved.

It was a squat old thing, black wood, with brass handles, which the two of them had pushed against the hallway-side wall of the front room because it was too heavy to get up the stairs. Dave knew the gap. He had measured it with his own knuckles the day they moved in, because it had seemed to him that a piece of furniture that heavy ought to be flat to the wall and it would not go.

Three inches. He crouched and put his hand in the space, up against the wallpaper, and felt the air there. Three inches, clean and even the whole length of it, while the boards between the wall and the sideboard held every particle of dust that had ever been there, undisturbed.

He sat back on his heels in the dark. Somewhere above him the house settled, soft as a sleeper turning.

“Right,” he said, to nobody, and to the room. “Right.”

He went back up the stair without his water. He slept badly. In the morning, before he woke his partner, he went down and pushed the sideboard back against the wall, and stood with his shoulder against the wood, pressing it as though the firmness of his own hands might be a thing the house respected.

## Chapter Three: The Name on the Stone

The third morning, the mist had climbed into the yews.

Dave had begun to walk more slowly through the cemetery. He told himself it was the uneven ground, the flat slabs that tipped underfoot, but the truth was that the old rows pulled at him. The mist lay along them in a dense white band, filling the gaps between the markers, and the names there had been worn down to the ghosts of letters. He stood at the gate longer than he needed to, one hand on the cold iron, and looked in.

That was when he saw the stone.

It was half sunk at the corner of the oldest row, a low slab worn smooth as a doorstep, and the mist had thinned just enough around its face to show the cutting. He stepped off the path and crossed the wet grass. The stone was furred with lichen, the letters shallow, but his eye caught the shape of them.

ELLERY.

Below it, smaller: *Mary Ellery. Beloved.*

He crouched. The date had worn away to a smear, but the name was clear enough. He read it three times, and on the third reading the back of his neck went cold.

He had signed the deed at the solicitor’s in June. He remembered the paper, the thick cream envelope, the way the woman had turned it round to face him and said, *the Ellery property*, as though the house were still a person’s.

He stood up slowly. The mist sat around his knees. Somewhere beyond the yews a dog barked twice and stopped.

“Right,” he said, quietly, to the stone. “Right.”

---

At home, the sideboard was out from the wall again.

Dave stopped in the front-room doorway with his coat still on. Three inches, clean and even, the whole length of it. The dust between the wood and the wallpaper lay undisturbed, grey and soft, exactly as it had the night before. Exactly as it had when he had pushed the sideboard back with his shoulder and stood there pressing it flat, as if firmness might mean something to a house.

He went to find his partner.

“Come and look at this.”

They were at the kitchen table with a cup of coffee and the crossword, and they came, because they always came at first, because that was still the shape of the two of them. But Dave saw the look they put on as they crossed the hall, the small bracing look, the one that said *here we go*.

“There,” Dave said. “Three inches. Same as before.”

His partner looked at the gap for a moment. Then they sighed, set the coffee down, and put both hands against the sideboard’s end.

“It’s heavy,” Dave said.

“It’s on a runner.” They shoved, and the sideboard went back against the wall with a dull knock, and they dusted their palms on their jeans. “There. Done.”

“I pushed it back yesterday morning.”

“Then you must have moved it again.”

“I didn’t move it.”

“Dave.” They said his name kindly. That was the worst of it. “You did. You moved it yesterday and forgot, and now you’ve got yourself worked up.” They picked up the coffee and looked at the dust line, and something flickered across their face, there and gone. “It’s an old house. Things settle. You’re tired.”

“I’m not tired.”

“You’re up at two in the morning looking at furniture. That’s tired.”

“Something crossed the landing.”

“Something.” They smiled, and it was almost gentle, and it still had that little shine along the rim. “Something crossed the landing, and the chair turned round, and the sideboard’s walked three inches out from the wall, and the windows are dirty on the inside. Do you hear yourself, love?”

He did. That was the thing. He heard himself, and he sounded like a man making excuses for a house.

“I’m not saying it’s ghosts,” he said.

“Good. Because that would be the point where I’d start hiding the good scissors.”

They laughed. He laughed too, a half-beat late, and the sound sat wrong in his chest. Then they went back to the crossword, and Dave stood in the front room with the sideboard flat to the wall and the dust line still showing pale on the boards where it had been.

---

That night he went up late.

The hallway lamp was on, the small brass one on the half-moon table, and it threw a soft yellow pool across the runner. Dave had his hand on the newel post when the light dimmed.

Not off. Dimmed, the way a lamp does when something heavy crosses the circuit, a brown sagging of the glow. The hairs on his arm lifted. Above him, the stair turned up into darkness, and the cold in the hall gathered close.

“Dave.”

He did not move.

The voice came from halfway up, from the landing where the stair turned, and it was a woman’s voice, low and clear. It said his name once. It said it correctly, without the question his partner put on it now, without the old teasing drawl. Just *Dave*, the way he said it himself inside his own head, the way someone who had known him a long time might say it across a room.

The lamp steadied. The yellow pool came back.

He looked up the stair. There was nothing on the landing. There was a smell, faint and dry, like lavender kept too long in a drawer, and then that was gone too, and there was only the runner and the wallpaper and his own hand gripping the newel post hard enough to whiten the knuckles.

“Hello?” he said.

His voice sounded thin. The house gave him nothing back. Somewhere behind him the boiler ticked, and the stair boards rested, and the lamp burned on as though it had never faltered.

Dave stood at the bottom of his own stairs and felt the want move through him, hot and shameful and utterly unreasonable: that the voice would come again. Not the shadow, not the knock, not the cold. The voice. That it would say his name once more, and go on saying it, and that he would be heard.

He shook his head hard, as if to dislodge something, and went up to bed.

## Chapter Four: The Courtesy of the Hall

The silence did not arrive all at once. It settled the way dust settles, day by day, until a room that had seemed clean showed a grey nap over everything.

Dave did not decide to stop telling his partner things. He simply noticed, somewhere in the second week, that he had stopped, and that the not-telling had already grown a shape of its own.

At dinner he talked about the bakery, about the water pressure, about the fact that the third stair from the top had begun to whine under his weight and he could not find the loose board. He did not talk about the landing. He did not talk about the voice, or the fact that he had lain awake the night after hearing it with his heart going like a bird in a box, not from fear, and that this was the thing he could least afford to say aloud.

His partner noticed the change the way they noticed everything: obliquely, and with a joke.

“You’ve gone quiet,” they said, on the Thursday. “In the old place you used to narrate. I could have written a book about your thoughts on the pelican crossing.”

“Nothing to narrate.”

“Mm.” They looked at him over the rim of their glass. “No ghosts today, then.”

“No.”

“Shame. I was going to get you a little hat with a lamp on it.”

He laughed. It came out on time, which was something. But the laugh did not reach the place in him where the voice had spoken his name, and his partner heard the hollowness of it, and the silence after it went on a beat too long, and neither of them filled it.

By the following week they had developed a kind of evening. His partner took the kitchen table with the crossword and the radio, and Dave took the front room with a book he did not read. Each of them said, at some point, *I’m going up*, and the other said, *right, night*, and the two of them went up at different times, and lay on opposite sides of the bed with a negotiation of blankets, and in the morning were kind to each other over tea.

Separate rooms. Separate evenings. Nothing had been said that could not be taken back, and yet something had been said by the not-saying, and it hardened in the walls of the house like damp plaster going off.

---

He began talking to the hallway out of a kind of exasperation.

It started on a wet Tuesday, when the pocket of cold had been particularly bad, standing in the middle of the runner so that he had to walk around it to reach the stairs, and Dave was carrying a laundry basket and his arms were full and he was tired of it in a plain, uncomplicated way.

“Look,” he said to the hall at large. “I don’t know what you are. But the cold’s in my way and it’s making a draught in the front room. Would you mind?”

He had meant it as a joke. He had meant it to be heard by nobody, which was the only kind of joke he had left in this house.

The cold went out of the hall.

Not all at once. It thinned the way frost does under a warm hand — a little at the edges, then all of it, so that when he walked the runner to the stairs with his basket the air was merely an old house’s air, cool and still and entirely ordinary.

Dave stopped at the foot of the stair with his arms full of washing.

“Right,” he said, and the back of his neck was prickling. “Right. Well. Thank you.”

He went up and put the laundry away and sat on the edge of the bed for a long while with his hands on his knees.

The next morning he found the top drawer of the dresser by the stair had been closed. It had been open for a week — the runner he used, the little brass key for the back door, a torn thing he meant to mend — and now it was shut, flush and neat, and when he pulled it there was nothing inside worth mentioning. He stood with the drawer open and looked at it and could not remember a single reason why he should have closed it without noticing.

“You’re being polite,” he said to the hallway, half-mocking, half not. “Aren’t you.”

The house said nothing. But it had gone warm-ish, and it stayed warm-ish, and Dave found that warmth somehow more difficult to bear than the cold had been.

---

At the end of that week he walked the cemetery later than usual. The mist lay along the old rows, and he went to the corner of the row without deciding to, and stood at the half-sunk slab with the lichen on it.

“Mary Ellery,” he said aloud. “Beloved.”

The mist did not move. Somewhere in the yews a blackbird shifted its weight.

What he felt was not fear. That was the trouble. It was something more like an apology, and he did not know to whom he owed it.

“I’m sorry about the house,” he said, and felt foolish, and went on, because there was nobody to hear. “If it means anything. I don’t think I’ve been courteous about it.”

He walked home with the taste of the mist in his mouth and did not tell his partner where he had been or what he had said.

---

That night he came up the stairs slowly with the lamp brown above his head, and on the landing she was waiting.

Not motion this time. Not the wrongness at the edge of sight, not the shadow crossing left to right. She stood at the turn of the stair in the dimness, and the straitened light of the landing window lay across her.

A high-collared dress, dark, the collar of it severe and lovely against her throat. Her hair was gathered. Her hands were folded in front of her, wrists to wrists, and she was not looking at him but a little past him, as though she had been waiting some time and had found ways to pass the while.

Dave stopped on the last step but one.

He was not frightened. He was certain, later, that he should have been, and that he could not find it in himself to be, and that this in itself was the most frightening thing available.

“Hello,” he said.

She turned her face to him, and it was a face — pale, patient, with the fine lines at the eyes that are made by years of smiling or years of keeping things back; he could not tell which.

“You said it was in your way,” she said. “The cold.”

The voice was the voice from the stair. It was the voice that had said his name.

“It was.”

“It’s not now.”

“No.”

She inclined her head. It was not a nod. It was slower than that, and older, the way a woman is courteous at a doorway to someone who has come a long way. Dave felt the greeting land in his chest like a hand laid flat.

“I’m Dave,” he said, stupidly.

“I know.”

Behind her, the streaked window greyed and the mist pressed against the glass, and she was thinning in it — not dissolving, not vanishing; going the way a reflection goes when the light changes. The collar went first, then the gathered hair.

“Thank you,” he said, too late, at the empty landing, at the yellowish lamp.

He stood there with his hand on the banister for a long time. It smelled of dry lavender, faint, in a drawer too long shut.

Downstairs, his partner turned the radio up.

The grey went out of the screen and the fountain's blue light came up around me, and the first thing I did was look at the scoreboard the way you look at a bruise you already know is there. Four kills. Nineteen deaths. Our top inhibitor was a crater, and the lane beyond the crater was already black with minions queued for the first super wave.

I bought nothing. I had Four items already — Youmuu's, Duskblade, Profane Hydra, and the Lord Dominik's I'd finished right before the Baron fight went wrong — and I had boots with an enchantment that would not save me. There was no bruiser item in the shop for me. There never was.

"Thirty-one seconds on Rengar ult," I said out loud, to nobody. It was a habit. My mum had asked once why I talked to a screen. I told her I was counting debts.

"Kade's still dark," Sana said. Her voice was the same flat spreadsheet tone she used for everything, like she was reading a receipt. "Thirteen minutes now. He'll be back with a story."

"He'll be back with a mouthful of excuses and a wave he has to push," Ilya said. "The wave is always the alibi. The wave is the last friend of a man who cannot group."

"Minion wave top, twenty seconds," Sana said. "Patch messed the timers, they're stacking faster than last season. Bo, don't stand in the choke, they path through the choke."

Bo was counting. He always counted when he was scared, and he was always scared. "One-forty-one CS," he said. "One-forty-one. If I hit one-fifty I get my third item and we win. That's the omen. One-fifty."

"Bo," I said. "There is no omen. There's a wave coming."

"One-fifty," Bo said, quieter.

I ran out of the fountain with the ult timer ticking in the corner of my eye. That was what my whole game had become, in the end. Not the gold, not the scoreboard — the clock on the one button that let me be anywhere and then be gone. Rengar's ult was the only thing I owned in that game, and it was at twenty-two.

The minion wave hit the choke first. Two casters and a cannon, and I watched them shrug off Sana's ball and keep walking. Ilya stepped up past the inhibitor stump, which is a thing a support should never do, and said, "Well. I'm going to die. But I'm going to die with my hook up, and that's more than most men can say," and he threw it.

The hook came out of the fog like an accusation. It caught the Blitzcrank who had been creeping up behind Bo to grab him out of the backline, and it dragged him in, and Bo — who was at one-forty-six and had promised himself a fight at one-fifty — fired anyway, rockets screaming, the omen forgiven.

"Worth it," Ilya said, deadpan, as he got blown apart by the Draven two seconds later. "I'll be back in twenty. The enemy gets bored; that's their weakness. Nobody early-game comp wins if you refuse to lose fast."

Fourteen deaths. Twelve. The wave died between us.

LeBlanc was the one I wanted.

She'd been the reason the Baron went the way it did — she'd flanked through our jungle at twenty-four minutes and deleted Sana from a bush, and we'd gone in four-on-five and fed them the pit. She was greedy, and greed is a timer too. She came to the entrance of our jungle alone, thirty seconds after the wave died, because she wanted to cut the next one off before it formed. She wanted to be clever.

I was sitting in the brush. My ult had come up two seconds before.

"Rengar ult, up," I said. And then I said the thing I always say, the thing I've said ten thousand times on an overheating laptop in a bedroom that smells like dust and Monster: "Nobody follows me."

The leap was the whole character. I pressed the button and the world went quiet and I was already behind them, and there was no halfway version of the build I played — no shield item to save me if I missed, no HP bar to argue with. I killed them in one rotation or I was the corpse.

I landed on her. Q, Empowered Q, Profane, Duskblade — the numbers went up like a slot machine and her health bar simply left. She flashed into the bush and I was already there, because I'd seen her finger it, because Sana had called her flash timer out loud eleven minutes ago and I'd kept it in my head like a coin.

"LeBlanc dead," I said. "Ult, forty."

Nobody cheered. That's not what this team does. Bo said, "One-fifty-two," in a small proud voice. Sana said, "Top wave in fifteen, they've got the second one queued behind it, Kade's still dark." Ilya, dead in the fountain, said, "And so we continue to lose, but slightly less efficiently."

But I could feel it. The way the damage landed on a LeBlanc and she had to walk to lane instead of flying there. The way the map opened when the enemy had one less knife to put in my back. Full-damage Rengar didn't win by being safe. It won by making every squishy on their team do arithmetic every time they stepped into fog, and their team was nothing but squishy — Renekton, Lee Sin, LeBlanc, Draven, Blitzcrank, five glass windows and not one door.

"First super wave," Sana said. "It's the fat one. It's coming now."

I looked up the lane. The super minions came out of the dark like a bill arriving, three of them shoulder to shoulder, the top inhibitor beyond them dead and spitting. My ult was at thirty-one. Thirty.

"Hold the choke," I said. "I'm not here for the wave."

"You're never here for the wave," Ilya said, and it sounded, for once, almost like faith.

The wave crashed into the inhibitor stump. My ult was counting down.

26:20.

The first super minion came through the choke like a landlord. It had been eating our base for a week, it knew the way, and it did not care that four people were standing in front of it.

"Ball on the cannon," Sana said. "I'm going to drag it left, don't chase it, let the choke do the work."

She did not shout it. She never shouted anything. She said *ball on the cannon* the way you'd read out a bus timetable, and then the little orb went skipping across the floor of our base and pulled the whole wave sideways into the wall, and the casters turned to follow it like dogs turning to a whistle.

"One-fifty-three," Bo said, and shot the cannon.

"Lantern the front one, Ilya," I said. "Not me. Bo."

"Everyone wants the lantern," Ilya said, throwing it anyway. "Nobody wants to be the man who stands still."

The lantern came out green and Bo took it and Bo was suddenly not where the super minions thought he was, and the front of the wave broke on the inhibitor stump instead of on his face. My ult was at fourteen. Thirteen.

I ran the edge of the fight. That's all full-damage Rengar does before the button comes up — he runs the edge and he lies to himself about being useful. I threw a Q into a caster, took a fifth of my health from the return fire, and backed off into the fog of our own jungle with my heart going like a metronome set too fast.

"Renekton's flanking," Sana said. "He's at nine hundred gold off his GA. He wants to dive."

"He's at the age where men make mistakes," Ilya said, deadpan. "Twenty-six minutes is a long time to be a crocodile. Eventually you forget you were ever a threat."

"Kade's at fourteen minutes," Sana said, because it was on her screen and she was constitutionally incapable of not reading it out. "Fourteen and change. He's going to reconnect into a wave and tell us the wave was the reason."

"He will reconnect into five excuses and a dead top lane," Ilya agreed. "And he will blame the wave, and the wave will forgive him, because the wave is kind."

"Ult's up," I said. Because it was. Because that's what I said, every time, like a man announcing his own heartbeat.

And then the enemy came in the way useless comps always do at twenty-six minutes — too fast, because their whole identity was built on the clock being shorter than it was. Blitzcrank came out of the fog first with his hook hand up, because that was the plan, and the plan was a hook and nothing after the hook.

The hook missed Bo by a foot. Just a clean miss, out into the empty base, and Bo didn't even have to flash.

"One-fifty-eight," Bo said, in a voice like he'd survived a car crash.

"Blitz is naked for nineteen," Sana said. "Everyone count nineteen. Renekton's going in, he's going in on the turret—"

Renekton went in. He flashed over the choke and onto our nexus turret and he was suddenly a very lonely crocodile in a base with four people in it, because LeBlanc was hanging back at the mouth of the choke — she had no cooldowns worth dying for once her combo was gone, that's the whole disease of her — and Draven was following Renekton because Draven had never in his life said no to a fight.

"Draven alone," I said, and my hands were already doing the thing. "Nobody follows me."

I pressed the ult. The world went quiet and grey and I was on the far side of Draven before he finished turning, and there's no bruiser in the build, there's no armor, there's no negotiation — I hit him with everything and his health bar just left the building like it had somewhere better to be.

"Draven dead," I said. "Ult, forty-one. Renekton's on the turret, kill him, he's nothing now—"

Renekton was nothing now. That was the thing nobody in Silver understands about Renekton. He's a monster at eight minutes and at twenty-six he's a very angry man with a stun and no damage, and he was standing under our nexus turret with our turret shooting him and Sana's ball arriving and Ilya's flay coming down on his ankles like a verdict. He died. He died and he knew it was a bad idea before he did it, and that is the loneliest way to die in this game.

"Renekton dead. Wave's half," Sana said. "Rebuild the wave, don't chase, we've got the second one behind it in forty."

The wave died.

That's the thing about super minions that nobody believes until they've done it: if the wave dies, it dies. All of it. The huge ones, the little ones, the whole terrible family, and then there's just the floor of your base and the corpses and the four of you, breathing, alive, with the score still 7–19 and your top lane still a graveyard.

"We didn't lose," Bo said. He said it like he was trying the word out. "One-sixty CS. One-sixty." He paused. "One-sixty-two. I'm going to hit two hundred and then I'm going to buy a GA and then I'm going to be a real boy."

"You're going to die," Ilya said, "but you'll die with your crit." He collected the last soul off a fallen caster and said nothing else about it, which is how Ilya says he's pleased.

I stood in the wreckage of the choke with my ult at thirty-eight and looked at the map, and the map was the same as it had been ten minutes ago and completely different, because the enemy had spent a Baron and one super wave and a Draven, and we had lost nothing but minions.

"Second wave queued," Sana said, flat as ever. "Top lane, forty seconds. And Kade's reconnect icon is doing the thing. It's flickering. He's coming back or he's not, and either way he's going to have a story."

I watched the icon flicker in the corner of my screen. Fifteen minutes was almost up. I thought about what Kade would say when he got back — *the connection, man, the connection was gone, and the side wave was pushing, I had to push it* — and I thought about the second super wave, already walking, already in the dark between the inhibitors.

"Let him come back," I said, and my ult started counting. "We're just getting started."

Thirteen Minutes

26:40.

The second wave was in the dark between the inhibitors, and Kade was still dark with it.

“Thirteen minutes and change,” Sana said, in the voice she used for bus timetables. “His icon hasn’t flickered in a while. Either he’s coming back or his router has achieved enlightenment.”

“He’ll come back with a story,” Ilya said. “They always come back with a story. The story is the only item they can afford.”

We held the choke with four.

That was the whole plan, and it was not a good plan. Sana put her ball on the cannon and dragged the wave left, into the wall, where the casters turned like dogs hearing a whistle. Bo stood behind the inhibitor stump and counted. “One-seventy-four. One-seventy-five. One-seventy-six.” Each number came out like he was blowing on a bruise. Ilya hooked the front super minion off Bo’s face and said, “I’m going to die, but I’m going to die with my hook up,” and did not die, which disappointed him.

I ran the edge with my ult at fourteen. Thirteen. Full-damage Rengar does not tank waves. Full-damage Rengar waits in the fog and lies to himself about being useful until the button comes up.

When it did, at 27:18, I used it on LeBlanc. She had come to the mouth of our jungle to be clever again, to cut the next wave before it formed, and I landed on her from the brush with everything I had. Q, empowered Q, Profane, Duskblade. Her health bar left the building. She flashed into the wall and I was already there, because Sana had called her flash timer eleven minutes ago and I kept those things like coins.

“LeBlanc dead,” I said. “Ult, forty.”

“They’re slowing down,” Sana said. “They should be. They’re an early-game comp at twenty-seven minutes with no tank and one hook. Every second we’re alive is a second their clock runs out.”

“The clock is a cruel god,” Ilya said, “and he hates Lee Sin.”

We held. The wave broke on the stump. Bo hit one-eighty. My ult came up again at 27:58, and I used it on Renekton, who had flashed over the choke to dive Bo and was suddenly a very lonely crocodile in a base with four people in it. He died mid-stun. His health bar didn’t so much fall as resign.

“Renekton dead,” I said. “Ult, forty-one.”

“Kade’s icon,” Bo said. “It’s doing the thing.”

I looked. In the corner of my screen, the reconnect icon flickered once, twice, and then went green.

28:30.

“GUYS.” Kade’s voice hit my headset like a dropped pan. “Guys, I’m back, I’m back, the router—my little brother was downloading a game, the whole house went down, I couldn’t even—I’m back. What did I miss? Are we winning? We’re winning, right? I have Darius. I have Ghost. I’m going to run at somebody.”

“You were gone exactly fifteen minutes,” Sana said. “I counted.”

“Fifteen minutes is nothing,” Kade said. “Fifteen minutes is a nap. Okay, okay, I’m pushing this side wave, it’s huge, it’ll crash into their tier two and then—”

“Kade.” My voice came out flatter than I meant. “Turn around. The second super wave is still at the choke.”

“It’s a huge wave, though.”

“It’s a huge wave,” I said, “and you’re the only person on this team who can stand in front of a super minion without becoming a red mist. Turn around.”

There was a pause filled with the sound of Darius’s axe dragging on stone. Then Kade said, “…Fine. Fine! I’m coming. I’m the tank. I’m the big man. Daddy’s home.” He laughed like he was trying to sell us something. “God, I missed you guys. Ilya, did you die while I was gone?”

“Twice,” Ilya said. “It was restful.”

Kade came into the choke at 28:40 with his health bar full and his Ghost up, and he did the one thing Darius is actually good for at twenty-eight minutes: he walked into the wave and let it hit him. He tanked the shots meant for our nexus turret, then the turret shot over his shoulder while Bo stood behind him and counted. One-ninety. One-ninety-one. The super minions broke on Kade’s face and the wave died around him.

“Wave cleared,” Sana said. “They’re backing off. Lee Sin’s in the river, he’s warding Baron—no flash, he flashed top at twenty-four.”

My ult came up at 28:52.

“Rengar ult, up,” I said. “Nobody follows me.”

I pressed it. The world went grey and quiet and I was behind Lee Sin before he finished the ward animation. Full-damage Rengar is not a duel; it’s a bill collector. I hit him with everything and his health bar left like it had been called for dinner. He kicked me into the wall, which was the only thing he had time for, and then he was dead and I was standing in the river with a shutdown’s worth of gold and my ult at forty.

“Lee Sin dead,” I said. “Shutdown. Ult forty.”

“Blitz is coming to ward,” Sana said. “He’s alone. He thinks Lee Sin is still alive.”

Blitzcrank came out of the fog with his hook hand up and his little robot legs going, and Ilya’s hook came out of our jungle and caught him by the throat. No windup. No warning. “I’m going to die,” Ilya said, “but I’m going to die with my hook up,” and then Bo shot Blitzcrank in the face and Blitzcrank died before he could press a button.

“Blitz dead,” Sana said. “They’re giving up Baron vision. They just gave us the whole river.”

We took it. We warded the pit and the mouth of their jungle, and for the first time in the game the dark belonged to us.

Then, at 29:00, the third wave spawned. It was the big one, the one the game saves for people who have been holding too long: four super minions, a cannon, a train of casters coming down the top lane like a receipt for everything we’d spent.

And Sana said, “They’re on Baron.”

Her voice didn’t change. It never did. “They’re starting it now. Third wave top, biggest one. They’re racing us.”

“Pit,” Sana said. “Go.”

29:00.

"Pit," Sana said. "Go."

We went. Four of us into the river mouth, Kade first because Kade is always first now that he's decided he's the tank, Bo behind him counting under his breath, "two-oh-two, two-oh-three," Ilya trailing with his lantern already out like a man carrying an umbrella into a storm he's certain is coming.

The enemy peeled off Baron before we got there. That's the thing about an early-game comp at twenty-nine minutes — they don't want the fight, they want the objective, and when the objective gets contested they get confused about which one they wanted. Lee Sin kicked out of the pit first, then Renekton, then the whole glass family spilled into the river mouth where the ground is narrow and there's nowhere to run.

"Draven's got his axes up," Sana said. "LeBlanc has no flash — I've told you this, I told you at twenty-two—"

"Rengar ult, fourteen," I said. Thirteen. Twelve.

We fought ugly. That's the only kind of fight we ever had. Kade ran at Renekton and Renekton ran at Bo and Bo ran backward counting, "two-oh-six, two-oh-seven," and Ilya hooked Renekton in the ribs and said, "I'm going to die," and did not, and the pit boiled.

"Ult's up," I said. "Nobody follows me."

I pressed it. Grey, quiet, and I was behind LeBlanc before she finished her clone. Full-damage Rengar is a bill collector, and she owed me. Q, empowered Q, Profane, Duskblade. Her health bar left the building. She didn't flash — she had no flash, Sana had counted it out loud eleven minutes ago — and she just stood there in her little grey dress and died with her combo half-cast.

"LeBlanc dead," I said. "Ult, forty."

"Baron's resetting," Sana said. "They're backing off the pit — they've lost the damage, they can't do it now. But Vex—"

"I know," I said.

The third wave was in the base.

I could see it on the minimap the way you see the bill on the counter: four super minions and a cannon and a train of casters walking into our open top lane, our nexus turret with its little health bar getting smaller.

"Draven's still up," Sana said. "He's greedy, he's going to follow—"

Draven followed. Of course he did. Draven has never in his life said no to a fight, and he came around the back of the river mouth with his axes spinning, and my ult was at thirty-one.

Thirty. Twenty-nine.

"Kade, hold him," I said. "Hold him for nineteen."

"I'm holding!" Kade shouted, which is what Kade says when he's about to die. He Ghosted into Draven's face and ate the axes and did not die, because Darius at twenty-nine minutes has a health bar like a filing cabinet.

The ult came up. "Rengar ult, up."

I went. Grey, quiet, Q, Q, Profane — and Draven's health bar left like it had somewhere better to be, and his axes fell on the floor of the river and stopped spinning.

"Draven dead," I said. "Ult, forty. Go home. Go home now."

We ran.

That's the part nobody puts in the highlight reel — four people sprinting down the river with a super wave eating their base, boots and Ghost and Sana's ball pinging ahead of us. Baron reset behind us. We hadn't taken it. We'd only stopped them taking it, which is a different and worse thing, but it was the only thing we could afford.

We hit the choke at 30:10.

The wave was already inside. Four super minions shoulder to shoulder, the cannon behind them, casters flooding the gap where the inhibitor used to be. And Kade did the only thing Kade is truly good for: he walked into it. He walked into four super minions and let them hit him, and his health bar went down like a countdown, and he shouted, "I'm tanking! I'm tanking! Somebody do something!"

"Ball on the back line," Sana said, and dragged the casters into the wall, where they turned like dogs at a whistle.

"Lantern the cannon," Ilya said. "Or don't. I'll die either way." He lanterned Kade out of the middle of the wave, hooked the front super minion off Bo's face, and said nothing else about it.

Bo counted. "Two-ten. Two-eleven. Two-twelve." Each number a small prayer. He shot the cannon and the cannon came apart and the wave started to fold in on itself.

I ran the edge with my ult at thirty-eight. Full-damage Rengar does not tank waves. I threw Q into a caster, took a third of my health, backed into the fog, and waited like a man waiting for a bus he knows is late.

The wave broke at 30:40. All of it. The huge ones, the little ones, the whole terrible family — and then there was just the floor of our base and the four of us breathing, and Kade at a hundred and forty health saying, "See? See? I tanked it. I'm the tank."

"You're a wall with a mouth," Ilya said.

"Push," Sana said. "They're all dead or recalling. First time all game we can push. Bot inhibitor — go bot, it's the closest, it's the only one not behind two turrets."

We pushed out. That was the strange part, walking out of our base instead of into it. The map opened like a hand unclenching. Kade went to push the top wave because of course he did, and then actually turned around when I shouted, and we went bot as five.

The enemy bot inhibitor came down at 31:20 like a fence post. Bo hit it, Kade hit it, I hit it, and it fell, and the sound it made was the best sound in the game.

"First inhibitor," Sana said. "Ours, I mean. Our first. They respawn in ten. Baron's up in thirty."

"Second inhibitor," I said. "Mid. That's the real one. Take mid and the nexus turrets open up and then it's just a race we can actually win."

"Backdoor," Ilya said, in his flat doom voice, and for once it didn't sound like doom at all. "The boy wants to backdoor. Of course he does. Nobody follows him."

"Nobody follows me," I said, and my ult started counting.
